claim: [GoDaddy Airo AI Builder] Free-tier staging URL is a long autogenerated godaddysites.com subdomain (site-nwujq32p6.godaddysites.com / yourbusinessname.godaddysites.com), with no rename control.
correction: This conflates two different GoDaddy products. (1) Airo AI Builder has NO free-tier staging URL at all — the Free plan cannot publish: 'you'll need to upgrade to a paid plan if you want to publish your website.' Publishing starts at Starter ($9.99/mo, 1 published project). (2) Airo AI Builder does not publish to godaddysites.com. A published Airo AI Builder project lands on *.airoapp.ai — the reviewer's live demo was https://eduflow.c39.airoapp.ai/, i.e. the pattern [projectname].[code].airoapp.ai. (3) godaddysites.com is the subdomain for Websites + Marketing / GoDaddy Website Builder, a separate legacy product — and the cited hostadvice article ('How to Use GoDaddy Website Builder') is about that product, not Airo AI Builder. The quoted verdict ('This subdomain is not viable for a professional business presence and will not help your SEO') is genuine but applies to W+M's free plan. Correct comparison against Remixer's editable *.remixer.app subdomain: Airo AI Builder gives you no free published URL whatsoever, which is a harsher gate than a bad subdomain — the point survives, the mechanism stated does not.

claim: Airo offers free one-click security, SEO and code-quality scans, with repairs billed
correction: The SEO scan is not free. The cited source states 'the scan itself is free, but the repairs use AI credits' for the security scanner, then explicitly contradicts the SEO half: 'The SEO and legal ones cost credits, but there is a QA one that's free — or at least it was when I ran it.' So the correct picture is: security scan free, QA/code-quality scan free (reviewer hedges that this may change), SEO and legal scans cost credits, repairs cost credits in all cases. The navigation path ('+' menu → Security → Run Analysis → Ask Airo to Fix) is confirmed. The 'scan-free/fix-paid' seam is real but narrower than claimed.

claim: All four paid Wix plans (Light $17, Core $29, Business $39, Business Elite $159 annual; $24/$36/$46/$172 monthly) include a free first-year domain, renewing at roughly $17.35/year; email sold separately
correction: The domain renewal figure is wrong. The cited source puts .com renewal at approximately $13.35/year, not $17.35/year. Everything else checks out: Light $17, Core $29, Business $39, Business Elite $159 on annual billing and $24/$36/$46/$172 monthly; a free custom domain for the first year on all premium plans; and email sold separately as an add-on (Google Workspace at roughly $6/user/month billed annually) rather than bundled the way Hostinger bundles mailboxes. The strategic conclusion — Wix funds its AI via hosting+domain subscription rather than metered credits — survives the correction.

claim: Google killed Firebase Studio on 19 March 2026, discontinuing the Cloud IDE and AI code generation; existing projects remain accessible until March 2027
correction: Nothing was killed on 19 March 2026. Google's own sunset doc gives the timeline as: 19 March 2026 — 'Sunset announcement, and migration tools start rolling out to Firebase Studio'; 22 June 2026 — 'New workspace creation and user signup are disabled. You can continue to work in and migrate existing workspaces'; 22 March 2027 — 'Firebase Studio is shut down, and all remaining data is permanently deleted and cannot be recovered.' So as of today (13 August 2026) Firebase Studio is still running for existing workspaces, with the Cloud IDE and AI code generation still functional — only new signups are closed. The claim also under-describes the consolidation: Google names two successors, Google AI Studio for browser-based prototyping (the right retarget for the App Prototyping agent) and Google Antigravity for local, code-first agentic workflows — not AI Studio alone. The '3 free workspaces, up to 30 via the Google Developer Program' detail was not verified.

claim: Category sweep pricing for Replit, Figma Make, Wix, Hostinger Horizons, Framer, Webflow, Emergent, Rocket.new, Tempo, Softr, Google AI Studio/Firebase Studio, Claude Artifacts, ChatGPT Canvas/Sites
correction: One clear factual error inside an otherwise strong sweep. FIREBASE STUDIO DID NOT SHUT DOWN 19 MARCH 2026 — it is still operating as of today. Google's own migration doc shows a phased sunset: new workspace creation and signups disabled 22 June 2026, users have until 22 MARCH 2027 to migrate, and full shutdown with data deletion occurs in 2027. The claim appears to have transposed the 2027 migration deadline into a 2026 shutdown date. Capabilities are being folded into Google AI Studio and Antigravity; core Firebase services (Firestore, Auth, App Hosting) are unaffected. CONFIRMED against primary sources: Hostinger Horizons Free/Explorer $6.99 (reg $9.99)/Starter $13.99 (reg $19.99)/Hobbyist $39.99 (reg $55.99) with 5/30/70/200 credits, 1/1/25/50 sites, 0/1/2/5 mailboxes, free domain from Starter, and the verbatim AI-credit sentence. Replit Starter free with daily Agent credits, Core $20 annual/$25 monthly with $25 credits, Pro $95 annual/$100 monthly with $100 credits, 5/15 collaborators, 2/10 parallel agents, 28-day rollbacks, effort-based pricing appearing as an undefined FAQ heading. Figma 3,000/3,500/4,250 full-seat and 500 Starter with 150/day, enforcement 18 March 2026, packages from 11 March 2026, PAYG by Q2 2026. Framer allowances and Wix $17/$29/$39/$159 annual with Light as the first custom-domain tier. Emergent $0/10, $20/100, $200/750, $300/1,250 with 50 credits per active deployment per month. Google AI Studio name.ai.studio subdomains announced 10 July 2026, free and first-come-first-served. ChatGPT Canvas removal on 28 May 2026. ALSO UNCONFIRMED: Hostinger's '7-day free trial with no payment info' — the pricing page advertises a permanently free plan with no card plus a 30-day money-back guarantee, not a 7-day trial. Figma's '~15,000 credits for ~$350' is not among the listed packages (5,000/$120, 7,500/$180, 10,000/$240). Rocket.new, Tempo and Softr figures could not be reached at their pricing pages and remain unverified, as the claim itself concedes.

claim: Base44 undocumented runtime ceilings: 150 ops/min, 5,000-item request cap, 3-min automation cutoff, 5-min backend function limit, max 50 backend functions, no user backups/SQL/indexing
correction: Every one of these numbers traces to a single adversarial third-party source (escapebase44.com), which itself concedes the 150 ops/min figure 'isn't documented anywhere.' The page does say what the claim reports — 5,000 items per request with silent truncation, automations 'cut off at 3 minutes', functions limited to '5 minutes', 'at most 50 backend functions', and no self-serve backups, direct SQL, or index control. But none of it appears in Base44's own documentation, there is no second independent source, and the publisher has an obvious incentive to portray the platform as production-unready. The claim's own 'treat as unverified' hedge is the correct posture; these figures should not be cited as fact or used for competitive benchmarking without hands-on confirmation.

claim: GoDaddy Airo has no documented keyboard shortcuts or command palette anywhere
correction: This is an absence claim, which is the hardest category to establish and the easiest to get wrong. GoDaddy's own help and product pages returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching, so the primary documentation could not be inspected; the only support is a third-party review of a SIBLING product (Websites + Marketing) listing 'lacks keyboard shortcuts' as a limitation, which does not transfer to Airo AI Builder. Failure to find documentation of shortcuts is not evidence that none exist — undocumented shortcuts are common, and GoDaddy's docs are not exhaustive. Treat as an untested hypothesis requiring hands-on confirmation in the product.

claim: GoDaddy Airo has no inline diffs, no file chips, no per-message revert; recovery is only via History and Backups
correction: Another absence claim resting on documentation that could not be retrieved — the cited GoDaddy help article (help/build-a-custom-app-or-site-with-airo-ai-builder-42824) returned HTTP 403, as did godaddy.com/airo/ai-builder. Nothing was found that affirmatively describes a diff view, changed-file chips, per-message rollback or a chat/agent toggle, but nothing was found ruling them out either, and the primary source is exactly the one that could not be read. The positive half of the claim — that recovery runs through a separate History list and Backups — is plausible and consistent with GoDaddy publishing a dedicated backup/restore doc, but was not directly confirmed. Requires in-product verification.

claim: GoDaddy Airo radii are bimodal: full-pill for AI/entry surfaces, ~8-12px for working chrome
correction: This is a visual design observation sourced to a single marketing screenshot hosted on GoDaddy's CDN (images.ctfassets.net). Pixel-level radius values cannot be confirmed through text search or page fetching, the underlying product pages returned 403, and a static promotional image cannot establish a systematic design rule across entry versus builder states. The interpretive leap — that the pill-to-rounded-rect shift 'maps exactly onto' a marketing-mode to work-mode transition — is an inference layered on an unmeasured observation, not a verified finding. If this matters for design benchmarking, measure it in the live product or in DevTools rather than citing it.

claim: GoDaddy Airo frames mobile as an output property, not an authoring environment; builder is desktop-only
correction: The specific verbatim quotes attributed to godaddy.com/airo/ai-builder ('Airo AI Builder focuses on web applications, but you can build mobile-responsive web apps...' and 'All AIRO-generated websites are mobile-friendly by default') could not be confirmed — that page returned HTTP 403 to fetching. Indirect corroboration exists that Airo treats mobile as an output quality: its pre-launch QA agent is documented as verifying mobile responsiveness alongside load speed and security. But that supports only the weaker reading. The load-bearing part of the claim — that the builder itself is desktop-only as an authoring surface — was not established by any source found, and the strategic conclusion about a mismatch with trade-business users rests entirely on it.
